                                   4                                   UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   5                                  NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   6

                                   7       LUCY YE, et al.,                                  Case No. 26-cv-01744-KAW
                                   8                    Plaintiffs,
                                                                                             ORDER RE 6/8/2026 DISCOVERY
                                   9              v.                                         LETTERS
                                  10       UBER TECHNOLOGIES, INC.,                          Re: Dkt. Nos. 33, 34
                                  11                    Defendant.                           [Discovery Letter Nos. 1, 2]
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           Plaintiffs Lucy Ye, Julia Fleming, and Jacqueline Clay filed the instant case against
                                  14   Defendant Uber Technologies, Inc., asserting that Defendant falsely advertises arrival times and
                                  15   charges a price premium for “faster” pickup times. (First Amend. Compl. (“FAC”) ¶¶ 23-24, 29.)
                                  16   Plaintiffs also seek declaratory relief that Defendant’s arbitration clause is unconscionable. (FAC
                                  17   ¶ 6.) On April 24, 2026, Defendant filed a motion to compel arbitration. (Dkt. No. 22.) On June
                                  18   8, 2026, the parties filed discovery letters concerning Plaintiffs’ discovery requests related to the
                                  19   alleged unconscionability of the arbitration clause.1 (Discovery Letter No. 1, Dkt. No. 33;
                                  20   Discovery Letter No. 2, Dkt. No. 34.) On June 12, 2026, Defendant filed a renewed motion to
                                  21   compel arbitration. (Dkt. No. 35.)
                                  22           The Federal Arbitration Act (“FAA”) “calls for a summary and speedy disposition of
                                  23   motions or petitions to enforce arbitration clauses.” Moses H. Cone Mem’l Hosp. v. Mercury
                                  24   Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1, 29 (1983). To this end, the “FAA provides for discovery . . . in
                                  25   connection with a motion to compel arbitration only if ‘the making of the arbitration agreement or
                                  26   the failure, neglect, or refusal to perform the same be in issue.’” Simula, Inc. v. Autoliv, Inc., 175
                                  27
                                       1
                                  28     The footnotes in the discovery letters fail to comply with Civil Local Rule 3-4(c)(2), which
                                       requires that footnotes be in 12 point type or larger.
                                         Case 4:26-cv-01744-KAW              Document 40       Filed 07/28/26     Page 2 of 4




                                   1   F.3d 716, 726 (9th Cir. 1999) (quoting 9 U.S.C. § 4.) Following Simula, however, both “[d]istrict

                                   2   courts in the Ninth Circuit and the Ninth Circuit itself have allowed a party opposing a motion to

                                   3   compel arbitration to conduct discovery relevant to the issue of unconscionability.” Meyer v. T-

                                   4   Mobile USA Inc., 836 F. Supp. 2d 994, 1007 (N.D. Cal. 2011); see Hoffman v. Citibank, N.A., 546

                                   5   F.3d 1078, 1085 (9th Cir. 2008) (remanding case to district court to expand the record on

                                   6   procedural unconscionability); Gilbert v. Bank of Am., No. C 13-01171 JSW (LB), 2014 U.S. Dist.

                                   7   LEXIS 165690, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 26, 2014) (permitting discovery as to procedural

                                   8   unconscionability); McArdle v. AT&T Mobility LLC, No. C 09-1117 CW (MEJ), 2013 U.S. Dist.

                                   9   LEXIS 40002, at *4-5 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 21, 2013) (acknowledging that discovery as to

                                  10   unconscionability is permissible).

                                  11          Defendant argues that discovery as to unconscionability is never permissible, but

                                  12   Defendant’s cited cases do not support this proposition. (Discovery Letter No. at 4-5.) For
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   example, Driskill v. Experian Info. Solutions, Inc. does not address the issue of discovery as to

                                  14   unconscionability at all. See 753 F. Supp. 3d 839, 848-49 (N.D. Cal. 2024) (denying request for

                                  15   discovery related to the plaintiff’s assent to arbitration, including seeking experts regarding the

                                  16   likelihood of consumer confusion and a consumer study of what consumers understood). Other

                                  17   cases acknowledge that courts have permitted discovery as to unconscionability, but that the

                                  18   discovery requested by the plaintiff did not actually provide information necessary to the court’s

                                  19   determination of unconscionability. E.g., Loewen v. Lyft, Inc., No. 15-cv-01159-EDL, 2015 U.S.

                                  20   Dist. LEXIS 191445, at *9, 15 (N.D. Cal. June 12, 2015) (finding that courts have permitted

                                  21   discovery as to unconscionability but that the plaintiffs failed to explain why the requested

                                  22   discovery would support an unconscionability argument); Hodsdon v. DirecTV, LLC, No. C 12-

                                  23   02827 JSW, 2012 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 160638, at *21 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 7, 2012) (same); Lag Shot

                                  24   LLC v. Facebook, Inc., 545 F. Supp. 3d 770, 781 (N.D. Cal. 2021) (denying discovery regarding

                                  25   other advertisers’ attempts to opt out because “whether other users made successful attempts to opt

                                  26   out of the arbitration agreement has no bearing on their own failure to do so”).

                                  27          In short, courts have permitted discovery as to unconscionability. The next issue, however,

                                  28   is whether Plaintiffs’ requested discovery falls within the scope of permissible discovery. A
                                                                                          2
                                         Case 4:26-cv-01744-KAW            Document 40         Filed 07/28/26      Page 3 of 4




                                   1   review of the case law demonstrates that while discovery as to unconscionability is permissible,

                                   2   the scope of that discovery is very limited. For instance, multiple courts have limited discovery to

                                   3   whether the plaintiff’s specific agreement was unconscionable, finding that discovery as to

                                   4   agreements, disputes, arbitrations, and lawsuits related to other customers were improper. See

                                   5   McArdle, 2013 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 40002, at *5-6; Lag Shot LLC, 545 F. Supp. 3d at 781.];

                                   6   Hodsdon, 2012 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 160638, at *22 (denying discovery where the plaintiffs focused

                                   7   on defendant’s “customers in general, rather than on the only relevant customers, which are

                                   8   Plaintiffs themselves”).

                                   9          Here, the vast majority of Plaintiffs’ proposed discovery is overbroad. For example,

                                  10   Plaintiffs seek the number of instances, broken out by year and applicable Terms of Service, in

                                  11   which Defendant’s customers or drivers sent a written notice of dispute to Defendant. (Discovery

                                  12   Letter No. 1, Exh. A (“Discovery Requests”) at 2-3.) It is unclear why every Terms of Service
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   would be relevant to the issue of whether the arbitration agreement applicable to Plaintiffs is

                                  14   unconscionable. Likewise, Plaintiffs seek discovery regarding drivers, while at the same time

                                  15   arguing that drivers are subject to a different set of arbitration terms. (See Discovery Letter No. 2

                                  16   at 3.) Plaintiffs also seek information about whether customers or drivers initiated arbitration or

                                  17   non-arbitration legal proceedings and the outcome of the proceedings, but it is not apparent why

                                  18   this would resolve any unconscionability issue. (See Discovery Requests at 3; Meyer, 836 F.

                                  19   Supp. 2d at 1007 (“Most of Plaintiff’s discovery requests do not relate to the validity of Plaintiff’s

                                  20   arbitration agreement with T-Mobile. Instead, they concern all agreements, disputes, arbitrations,

                                  21   and lawsuits relating to T-Mobile customers in California other than Plaintiff for the entire seven-

                                  22   year ‘relevant time period.’”).) Plaintiffs further seek information about the timeliness of an

                                  23   arbitration, but fail to explain why this relates to unconscionability, as opposed to Defendant’s

                                  24   general assertion that arbitration is faster -- it is unclear how speed relates to unconscionability.

                                  25   (See Discovery Requests at 4.) Plaintiffs likewise fail to explain why the rates paid by Defendant

                                  26   have any relevance to unconscionability. (See Discovery Requests at 5.) Finally, Plaintiffs seek

                                  27   all documents concerning Plaintiff Ye such as location data, but this request concerns the merits of

                                  28   the case and clearly falls well beyond the scope of unconscionability. See Coneff v. AT&T, No.
                                                                                          3
                                         Case 4:26-cv-01744-KAW               Document 40       Filed 07/28/26     Page 4 of 4




                                   1   C06-0944RSM, 2007 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 20502, at *8 (W.D. Wash. Mar. 9, 2007) (denying

                                   2   discovery that “relate[s] only to the merits of the dispute”).

                                   3          To be clear, this is not an exhaustive review of the overbreadth of Plaintiffs’ proposed

                                   4   discovery. Indeed, based on a brief review of the operative complaint and the discovery requests,

                                   5   the only discovery requests that at least seem connected (if still overbroad) to Plaintiffs’

                                   6   unconscionability arguments are Interrogatory Nos. 2 and 6 and Requests for Production 1 and 2.

                                   7   Ultimately, however, Plaintiffs have the burden of making a specific showing for how each

                                   8   discovery request is related to the unconscionability issue. Plaintiffs’ generic justifications do not

                                   9   meet that burden. See Coneff, 2007 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 20502, at *10 (“Plaintiffs’ conclusory

                                  10   arguments that all of their discovery requests relate to unconscionability does not defeat

                                  11   defendants’ valid objection to broad discovery at this time.”). Accordingly, the Court finds that no

                                  12   discovery is required at this time.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          The Court ORDERS the parties to meet and confer. The parties should discuss whether

                                  14   Plaintiffs still intend to seek discovery (and if so, whether Defendant agrees to produce such

                                  15   discovery), or if the parties should proceed with briefing the pending motion to compel arbitration.

                                  16   To the extent Plaintiffs have any discovery disputes, the parties shall file a joint discovery letter

                                  17   (or letters) which fully complies with the Court’s Civil Standing Order ¶ 14, including the required

                                  18   format. Plaintiffs will have the burden of explaining how each specific discovery request is

                                  19   related to the issue of unconscionability, specifically that of the delegation clause.

                                  20          IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                  21   Dated: July 28, 2026
                                                                                               __________________________________
                                  22                                                           KANDIS A. WESTMORE
                                  23                                                           United States Magistrate Judge
